questions.stem:
A 64-year-old man is admitted with fever, cough, and a lobar infiltrate. He cannot produce a sputum sample, and blood cultures are pending. He is started on a two-drug regimen that covers both common and atypical causes of community-acquired pneumonia. Two days later blood cultures grow a Gram-positive coccus that is susceptible to a narrow-spectrum agent, and his regimen is changed to that single drug.

The change made on day 2 is best described as which category of antibiotic use?
choices: Directed therapy
Combination therapy for synergy
Combination therapy to prevent resistance
Empiric therapy
Prophylactic therapy

explain.html:
Antibiotics are used in four ways: empiric therapy before culture results, directed (targeted) therapy after culture and susceptibility results, prophylaxis to prevent infection in a high-risk situation, and combination therapy in a few defined circumstances. Empiric therapy is chosen from the likely site and the most probable organisms, so it is usually broad and runs until cultures return. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia is the standard example, covering typical and atypical bacteria. Once the site, the organism and its susceptibilities are known, therapy is changed to a narrow-spectrum agent aimed at that isolate.

In this patient the two-drug regimen started without a sputum sample was empiric. The decisive finding is the blood culture with a known susceptibility on day 2, after which he is switched to one narrow agent, which is directed therapy. Narrowing limits side effects and the pressure that drives resistance, which is the goal of stewardship.
explain.table:
UseWhenExample
EmpiricBefore culture results, based on likely pathogensCeftriaxone plus azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia
Directed (targeted)Organism and susceptibilities known; narrow spectrum preferredOxacillin for MSSA bacteremia
ProphylacticHigh-risk procedure or state, no infection yetPreoperative cefazolin
CombinationPolymicrobial infection, synergy, or preventing resistance (mainly tuberculosis)Penicillin plus gentamicin for enterococci
why: Synergy is a reason to give two drugs together, and this patient was moved from two drugs to one.
Combinations to prevent resistance are used mainly for tuberculosis, and this change removed a drug.
Empiric therapy describes the first regimen given before cultures, not the change made once they returned.
Prophylaxis prevents infection in someone not yet infected, and this patient already has pneumonia with bacteremia.
explain.takeaway: Empiric therapy covers the likely pathogens before cultures return; once the organism and its susceptibilities are known, therapy is narrowed to a directed agent.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Differentiate the main clinical uses of antibiotics: Empiric, targeted, prophylactic, and combination therapy.

questions.stem:
A patient with an infected prosthetic device is treated with an agent reported as susceptible, at standard doses, yet the infection persists. The laboratory repeats testing and confirms the same result. Imaging and operative findings show a thick layer of organisms encased in matrix adherent to the device surface.

Which limitation of the reported laboratory value best explains this outcome?
choices: It is measured at 37 degrees Celsius
It does not reflect biofilm or efflux mechanisms
It is reported in mg/L rather than in micromoles per liter
It requires 18 to 24 hours of incubation
It is determined by broth microdilution

explain.html:
The MIC is a standardized in vitro measure of potency: broth microdilution, 18 to 24 hours of incubation at 37 degrees Celsius, on a pure isolate. It is the most elemental pharmacodynamic measure, but it has stated limits. It is a static measurement that does not track changing drug levels over time, it may not reflect resistance mechanisms like biofilm formation or efflux pumps, and an in vitro result may not predict in vivo efficacy under complex physiological conditions.

This patient's device is coated with a matrix-encased layer of organisms, a biofilm, and the repeat test still reads susceptible. That combination of a susceptible MIC and persistent clinical failure is what the biofilm limitation predicts. Infected devices are the setting where a reassuring laboratory result should not end the thinking about why therapy is failing.
why: Incubation at 37 degrees Celsius is part of the standard method, not a reason a susceptible drug fails.
The units of reporting do not change whether the drug works in the patient.
The 18 to 24 hour incubation delays the result but does not explain failure once a susceptible drug is given.
Broth microdilution is the gold standard method, not a shortcoming of the value.
explain.takeaway: A susceptible MIC can coexist with treatment failure because the test is static and in vitro and does not capture biofilm formation or efflux pumps.
explain.topic: Limitations of the minimum inhibitory concentration
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Interpret antimicrobial susceptibility testing: Explain MIC determination, breakpoint setting, and limitations of MIC.

rows.if_right: a stem asking the units in which the laboratory reports an MIC

rows.if_right: a critically ill patient whose therapy cannot wait the 18 to 24 hours a standard MIC takes

questions.stem:
A stewardship team builds a table for four agents. Agent 1 is a beta-lactam. Agent 2 is an aminoglycoside. Agent 3 is vancomycin. Agent 4 is a fluoroquinolone. They want to list the pharmacodynamic index that best predicts efficacy for each, so that dosing paradigms can be set.

Which assignment is correct?
choices: Agent 1 fT above MIC and agent 2 fCmax to MIC
Agent 3 fCmax to MIC and agent 4 fT above MIC
All four agents are best predicted by fCmax to MIC
Agent 1 fAUC to MIC and agent 3 fT above MIC
Agent 2 fT above MIC and agent 4 fCmax to MIC

explain.html:
Antibiotics fall into three pharmacodynamic groups by the index that best predicts efficacy. Beta-lactams follow fT>MIC, the share of time free drug stays above the MIC, so they are dosed frequently or by prolonged infusion. Aminoglycosides follow fCmax:MIC, the peak to MIC ratio, so they are given as high doses at low frequency. Vancomycin and fluoroquinolones follow fAUC:MIC, the free area under the curve over 24 hours relative to the MIC, an index that mixes time dependence (vancomycin) and concentration dependence (fluoroquinolones), so one drug can appear in more than one category.

Applied to the table, agent 1 (beta-lactam) is fT>MIC and agent 2 (aminoglycoside) is fCmax:MIC. Getting the index right is what lets the team pick the dosing paradigm for each drug.
explain.table:
AntibioticPD indexPost-antibiotic effectDosing paradigm
Beta-lactamsfT>MICMinimalHigher frequency, prolonged infusions
AminoglycosidesfCmax:MICProlongedHigh dose, low frequency
VancomycinfAUC:MICNot listedFlexible
FluoroquinolonesfAUC:MICProlongedFlexible, high dose
why: Vancomycin and fluoroquinolones are both predicted by fAUC:MIC, not by the peak or by time above the MIC.
Only the aminoglycoside among these four is predicted mainly by the peak ratio.
This reverses the beta-lactam and vancomycin indices.
Aminoglycosides are concentration dependent, and fluoroquinolones follow fAUC:MIC.
explain.takeaway: Beta-lactams are predicted by fT>MIC, aminoglycosides by fCmax:MIC, and vancomycin and fluoroquinolones by fAUC:MIC.
explain.topic: Matching the pharmacodynamic index to the drug
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Apply pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) principles: Explain PD indices (fT>MIC, fCmax:MIC, fAUC:MIC) and post-antibiotic effect.

rows.why: Vancomycin and fluoroquinolones are both predicted by fAUC:MIC, not by the peak or by time above the MIC.

rows.why: Only the aminoglycoside among these four is predicted mainly by the peak ratio.
rows.if_right: four aminoglycosides, such as gentamicin and tobramycin

rows.why: This reverses the beta-lactam and vancomycin indices.
rows.if_right: agent 1 being vancomycin and agent 3 a beta-lactam

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old woman is scheduled for an elective operation. She has no active infection, no allergies, and normal organ function. The surgical team plans a single intravenous dose of an agent active against common skin flora, given within 60 minutes before the incision.

Which statement best describes this use of the drug?
choices: Directed therapy guided by susceptibility results
Prophylaxis to prevent surgical site infection at a high-risk time
Empiric therapy for a suspected but unproven infection
Combination therapy chosen for a synergistic effect
Therapy chosen to prevent emergence of resistance

explain.html:
Prophylactic therapy is an antibiotic given to prevent infection during a procedure or in an immunocompromised state when the risk of infection is considerable. It differs from empiric therapy, which treats a suspected infection before cultures, and from directed therapy, which treats a known organism. Examples include amoxicillin before a dental procedure in a patient with a prosthetic valve and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a patient with AIDS and a low CD4 count. Cefazolin is the first-line agent for surgical prophylaxis in most procedures because it covers common skin flora such as staphylococci and is effective, safe and inexpensive.

This woman has no active infection and receives a single dose within 60 minutes before incision. Nothing is being treated, so the only category that fits is prophylaxis against surgical site infection.
why: Nothing has been cultured and there is no infection, so there are no susceptibilities to direct therapy.
Empiric therapy treats a suspected infection, and she has none.
Only one agent is given, so synergy does not apply.
Combination therapy to prevent resistance applies mainly to tuberculosis, not a single preoperative dose.
explain.takeaway: An antibiotic given before a procedure to prevent infection, such as cefazolin within 60 minutes of incision, is prophylactic therapy.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Differentiate the main clinical uses of antibiotics: Empiric, targeted, prophylactic, and combination therapy.

rows.why: Nothing has been cultured and there is no infection, so there are no susceptibilities to direct therapy.
rows.if_right: a switch to oxacillin after blood cultures grow MSSA

rows.why: Empiric therapy treats a suspected infection, and she has none.
rows.if_right: antibiotics started for suspected pneumonia before cultures return

rows.why: Only one agent is given, so synergy does not apply.
rows.if_right: penicillin plus gentamicin given together for an enterococcal infection

rows.why: Combination therapy to prevent resistance applies mainly to tuberculosis, not a single preoperative dose.
rows.if_right: a multidrug regimen started for tuberculosis

questions.stem:
A 74-year-old woman with reduced kidney function is treated for a serious Gram-positive infection with vancomycin. The team plans both an initial dosing decision and ongoing assessment. She also takes several other medications, and her allergy history and the cost of therapy were considered when the agent was chosen.

Which action represents monitoring rather than an initial host-factor consideration?
choices: Measuring serum drug concentrations at intervals during therapy
Checking for interactions with her other medications
Accounting for her age when selecting the agent
Considering the cost of the chosen regimen
Reviewing her allergy history before the first dose

explain.html:
Choosing and running antibiotic therapy has two phases. Host factors shape the initial selection and dose: allergies, age, pregnancy and nursing, renal and hepatic function, concomitant drug therapy, underlying disease states, and cost. Monitoring happens after therapy starts: measuring serum concentrations, setting the duration, and assessing response or therapeutic failure. The lecture's flow is that host factors influence dosing and then monitoring of the response adjusts therapy.

For this woman, her allergies, age, kidney function, other medications and cost were all weighed before the first dose. Only measuring serum drug concentrations at intervals during therapy belongs to monitoring, and vancomycin trough levels are the lecture's example, used for both efficacy and toxicity. Her reduced kidney function makes that monitoring especially important.
explain.table:
Host factors (initial choice)Monitoring (after starting)
Allergies, age, pregnancy and nursingSerum concentrations (vancomycin troughs)
Renal and hepatic functionDuration of therapy
Concomitant drugs, underlying disease, costResponse and therapeutic failure
why: Concomitant drug therapy is a host factor weighed when the drug is chosen.
Age is a host factor used in selecting and dosing the agent.
Cost is listed among the host factors that guide selection.
Allergy history is a host factor reviewed before starting.
explain.takeaway: Host factors (allergies, age, organ function, concomitant drugs, cost) guide the initial choice, while serum levels, duration and response assessment are monitoring.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Evaluate host-specific factors and monitoring strategies: Allergies, organ function, concomitant drugs, and therapeutic response.

questions.stem:
Two antibiotic pairs are tested against different organisms. Pair 1 is a cell wall-active agent plus an aminoglycoside against an enterococcus: neither drug kills the organism alone, but together they are bactericidal because wall damage increases intracellular uptake of the second drug. Pair 2 is a cell wall-active agent plus a bacteriostatic protein synthesis inhibitor against a pneumococcus, and killing is less than with the cell wall agent alone.

Which explanation accounts for the result with pair 2?
choices: The second drug increases uptake of the first into the cell
The bacteriostatic drug halts the growth the other drug needs
The two drugs bind the same ribosomal subunit and compete
The combination rapidly selects for efflux pump expression in vitro
The pneumococcus inactivates both drugs with a single enzyme

explain.html:
Most infections are treated with the single best agent, and combinations are reserved for polymicrobial infection, synergy, or preventing resistance in tuberculosis. Two drugs can be indifferent, synergistic, or, rarely, antagonistic. The classic synergy is penicillin plus gentamicin against enterococci: penicillin damages the cell wall, which raises intracellular uptake of gentamicin, and together they are bactericidal although neither works well alone. The classic antagonism is penicillin G plus tetracycline against S. pneumoniae meningitis.

Pair 2 follows that antagonistic pattern. A bactericidal cell wall agent kills only bacteria that are actively synthesizing wall, and the bacteriostatic drug halts growth, so the cell wall agent has nothing to act on and killing falls below what it achieves alone. In practice this is why a bacteriostatic agent is not added to penicillin for a serious infection such as pneumococcal meningitis.
explain.table:
InteractionPairMechanism
SynergyPenicillin plus gentamicin vs enterococciWall damage raises aminoglycoside uptake; together bactericidal
AntagonismPenicillin G plus tetracycline vs S. pneumoniae meningitisBacteriostatic drug stops the growth that cell wall killing requires
why: Increased uptake is the mechanism of synergy in pair 1, and it cannot explain the loss of killing in pair 2.
One drug in pair 2 acts on the cell wall, so the two do not compete for a ribosomal site.
Efflux selection is not the mechanism taught for this antagonism, which is about halted growth.
A single inactivating enzyme is not the explanation taught; the antagonism comes from halted growth.
explain.takeaway: A bacteriostatic drug antagonizes a bactericidal cell wall agent because cell wall killing requires actively growing bacteria, whereas a cell wall agent plus an aminoglycoside is synergistic against enterococci.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Differentiate the main clinical uses of antibiotics: Empiric, targeted, prophylactic, and combination therapy.

rows.if_right: a beta-lactamase producer that destroys the cell wall agent

questions.stem:
A clinical isolate is tested by gradient diffusion and the laboratory reports minimum inhibitory concentrations for five agents, in mg/L. A student concludes that the drug with the numerically lowest value must be the most effective choice for this patient.

[[labs 0]]

Which statement best corrects the student's reasoning?
choices: Gradient diffusion does not generate these values
Values below 1 mg/L always indicate resistance
Only broth microdilution results have clinical meaning
Lower values always indicate greater clinical efficacy
Values cannot be compared across different antibiotics

explain.html:
The minimum inhibitory concentration is the lowest antibiotic concentration that completely prevents visible growth in vitro, measured by broth microdilution (the gold standard), gradient tests, or automated systems. It reflects the potency of one drug against one isolate. Whether that number means susceptible, intermediate or resistant depends on a breakpoint, which is set separately for each drug from the MIC distribution of many isolates together with that drug's pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data. Because each antibiotic has its own breakpoint, MIC values often cannot be compared between antibiotics.

The student ranked five different drugs by their raw numbers, which is the exact error. Drug E's value of 0.25 mg/L is not better than drug B's value of 3 mg/L until each is read against its own breakpoint. The practical rule is to read every MIC as susceptible or resistant for that drug first, then choose using site of infection and achievable concentrations.
explain.table:
CategoryMeaning
SusceptibleHigh likelihood of success with standard dosing
IntermediateSuccess likely with increased dosing or concentration at the site
ResistantFailure likely even with increased exposure
why: Gradient strips are one of the standard phenotypic methods that generate these values.
A low value generally points toward susceptibility, not resistance, once read against the drug's breakpoint.
Broth microdilution is the gold standard, but gradient and automated methods also give clinically used values.
This is the student's own error restated, since a lower number does not mean better efficacy across different drugs.
explain.takeaway: An MIC must be interpreted against that drug's own breakpoint, so raw MIC values cannot be compared between different antibiotics.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Interpret antimicrobial susceptibility testing: Explain MIC determination, breakpoint setting, and limitations of MIC.

rows.if_right: a molecular method such as PCR, which detects resistance genes rather than producing an MIC

rows.if_right: a value above that drug's resistant breakpoint

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old man with chronic kidney disease is admitted with Gram-negative bacteremia, and gentamicin is added to his regimen. The pharmacy asks how the dosing interval should be set. Review of the drug shows that it is hydrophilic, has a low volume of distribution, undergoes minimal hepatic metabolism, and penetrates the central nervous system poorly.

Which property of this drug is most relevant to lengthening the dosing interval in this patient?
choices: Poor oral bioavailability requiring parenteral use
Extensive hepatic metabolism
High lipid solubility with a large volume of distribution
Elimination by renal glomerular filtration
Extensive binding to plasma proteins

explain.html:
Each antibiotic class has a pharmacokinetic profile across absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion, and the excretion route decides what organ failure changes the dose. Aminoglycosides have poor oral absorption and are given IV or IM, are hydrophilic and stay in extracellular fluid with a low volume of distribution and poor CNS penetration, undergo minimal hepatic metabolism, and are eliminated by renal glomerular filtration with a short half-life. That profile is why the lecture's note for the class is to adjust in renal impairment.

This man has chronic kidney disease, so filtration of gentamicin falls and the drug accumulates. The property that sets his dosing interval is therefore renal elimination, and the interval is lengthened to avoid toxicity. Renal function, not hepatic metabolism or protein binding, is the variable to check before every aminoglycoside dose.
explain.table:
ClassDistributionMetabolismExcretion
AminoglycosidesHydrophilic, extracellular, low VdMinimal hepaticRenal (glomerular filtration)
Beta-lactamsExtracellular, moderate VdMinimal hepaticRenal (most), biliary for ceftriaxone
MacrolidesLipophilic, good tissue penetrationExtensive hepaticBiliary
FluoroquinolonesLipophilic, high VdPartial hepaticRenal plus hepatic
RifampinWide tissue penetrationExtensive hepaticBiliary
why: Poor oral absorption explains why the drug is given IV or IM, not how often it is dosed.
Aminoglycosides undergo minimal hepatic metabolism, so this property does not exist for gentamicin.
Gentamicin is hydrophilic with a low volume of distribution, the opposite of this choice.
Protein binding affects the free fraction but is not the property that sets the interval in renal failure.
explain.takeaway: Aminoglycosides are hydrophilic, minimally metabolized and cleared by glomerular filtration, so their dosing interval is extended in renal impairment.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Apply pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) principles: Describe PK factors (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, tissue penetration).

rows.if_right: a macrolide or rifampin, whose dosing depends on extensive hepatic metabolism

rows.why: Gentamicin is hydrophilic with a low volume of distribution, the opposite of this choice.
rows.if_right: a fluoroquinolone, which is lipophilic with a high volume of distribution

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man with type 1 diabetes has a destructive lesion of the distal phalanx of the great toe on radiograph, and bone biopsy grows an oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod reported as susceptible to levofloxacin. He is started on intravenous therapy. At steady state the serum concentration of the drug is 40 mg/L. The teaching table for this drug lists a bone to serum ratio of 0.75.

Which value best estimates the drug concentration at the site of infection?
choices: 10 mg/L
20 mg/L
30 mg/L
40 mg/L
80 mg/L

explain.html:
An antibiotic that kills well in vitro is useless if it never reaches the site of infection at a high enough concentration. Penetration varies by tissue and by drug, so the primary site is a key variable and may require dose adjustment. Bone penetration is expressed as a bone to serum ratio, and the bone concentration is the serum concentration multiplied by that ratio. Lipophilic fluoroquinolones penetrate bone well (ciprofloxacin 0.35, levofloxacin 0.75), while hydrophilic beta-lactams (mostly 0.1 to 0.3), vancomycin (about 0.2) and aminoglycosides (predicted very low) penetrate poorly.

Here the serum level is 40 mg/L and the ratio is 0.75, so the bone concentration is 40 times 0.75, or 30 mg/L. That is the concentration actually acting on the organism in the phalanx. Choosing a lipophilic agent with a high ratio is why levofloxacin is a reasonable option for this osteomyelitis.
explain.table:
ClassBone to serum ratioWhy
Beta-lactams0.1 (oxacillin) to 1 (cefepime); most 0.1 to 0.3Hydrophilic, limited penetration
VancomycinAbout 0.20Higher doses needed
Fluoroquinolones0.35 (ciprofloxacin) to 0.75 (levofloxacin)Lipophilic, high Vd
AminoglycosidesData lacking, predicted very lowHighly hydrophilic
why: 10 mg/L would require a bone to serum ratio of 0.25, not the 0.75 given.
20 mg/L would require a ratio of 0.5.
40 mg/L assumes bone equals serum, a ratio of 1.
80 mg/L would require bone concentrations double the serum, which no listed drug reaches.
explain.takeaway: Bone concentration equals serum concentration times the bone to serum ratio, and lipophilic fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin (0.75) penetrate bone far better than hydrophilic agents.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Apply pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) principles: Describe PK factors (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, tissue penetration).

rows.if_right: a drug with a bone to serum ratio of 0.25 at a serum level of 40 mg/L

rows.why: 20 mg/L would require a ratio of 0.5.
rows.if_right: a drug with a bone to serum ratio of 0.5 at the same serum level

rows.if_right: a drug with a ratio of 1, the top of the beta-lactam range given for cefepime

questions.stem:
An infected patient is receiving a cell wall-active agent. The team considers giving the same total daily amount as fewer, larger doses. Laboratory work with this drug shows that raising the concentration beyond about four times the organism's minimum inhibitory concentration does not increase the rate or extent of killing, and that killing correlates with how long free drug stays above that value.

Which change in the regimen would best improve killing?
choices: Give larger doses less often to raise the peak
Use prolonged or continuous infusion of the same daily amount
Add a second drug with the same mechanism
Shorten the total duration of therapy
Target a peak to minimum inhibitory concentration ratio of 10 to 1

explain.html:
Pharmacodynamics groups antibiotics by what predicts killing: time above the MIC (fT>MIC), peak concentration to MIC (fCmax:MIC), or total exposure (fAUC:MIC). Beta-lactams are the classic time-dependent drugs, joined by clindamycin, macrolides and vancomycin. For these drugs, concentrations beyond about 4 times the MIC barely raise the rate or extent of killing, so the extent of killing depends on how long free drug stays above the MIC.

The stem gives exactly that profile, so the goal is to extend exposure, keeping free drug above the MIC for roughly 40 to 70% of the dosing interval (about 60 to 70% for cephalosporins, 50% for penicillin, 40% for carbapenems). Prolonged or continuous infusion of the same daily amount achieves that, which is why ceftazidime is given this way. Fewer, larger doses would waste drug on high peaks and leave long troughs below the MIC.
why: Larger, less frequent doses raise the peak, which adds little killing for a time-dependent drug.
A second drug with the same mechanism does not lengthen the time free drug stays above the MIC.
Shortening the course does nothing to improve killing within each dosing interval.
A peak to MIC target of 8 to 10 to 1 is the goal for concentration-dependent aminoglycosides.
explain.takeaway: Beta-lactams kill in a time-dependent way, so dosing aims to keep free drug above the MIC for 40 to 70% of the interval with frequent dosing or prolonged infusion.
explain.subject: Pharmacology
explain.objective: Apply pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) principles: Explain PD indices (fT>MIC, fCmax:MIC, fAUC:MIC) and post-antibiotic effect.

rows.why: Larger, less frequent doses raise the peak, which adds little killing for a time-dependent drug.
rows.if_right: an aminoglycoside, whose killing rises with the peak concentration

rows.why: A second drug with the same mechanism does not lengthen the time free drug stays above the MIC.
rows.if_right: a goal of synergy, which needs different mechanisms, such as penicillin plus gentamicin

rows.why: Shortening the course does nothing to improve killing within each dosing interval.
rows.if_right: a stewardship question about limiting duration of treatment

rows.why: A peak to MIC target of 8 to 10 to 1 is the goal for concentration-dependent aminoglycosides.
rows.if_right: an aminoglycoside dosed for concentration-dependent killing

questions.stem:
A patient with Gram-negative sepsis is to receive an aminoglycoside. The service uses an extended-interval regimen with a single large daily dose of 7 mg/kg, with a random level drawn between 6 and 14 hours after the dose to choose the interval from a nomogram. A trainee worries that drug concentrations will fall below the organism's minimum inhibitory concentration before the next dose.

Which property of this drug class best addresses that concern?
choices: Extensive hepatic metabolism that produces active metabolites
High protein binding that creates a drug reservoir
Lipophilicity that allows accumulation in tissue
Minimal renal clearance at high doses
A prolonged post-antibiotic effect on Gram-negative rods

explain.html:
Aminoglycosides are the classic concentration-dependent drugs: the higher the peak, the faster and more complete the killing, with a target peak to MIC ratio of 8 to 10 to 1. Keeping levels above the MIC for most of the interval is unnecessary and is discouraged because it raises adverse effects. The Hartford nomogram applies this with a single 7 mg/kg dose of gentamicin or tobramycin and one random level drawn 6 to 14 hours later to set the interval. The post-antibiotic effect is the time bacteria take to recover and resume growth after drug exposure, and it gives a buffer period during which concentrations can sit below the MIC without regrowth.

The trainee's worry is that levels fall below the MIC late in the interval. The aminoglycoside answer is their prolonged post-antibiotic effect against Gram-negatives, which keeps bacteria suppressed through that trough. That is what makes once-daily dosing effective while limiting toxicity.
why: Aminoglycosides undergo minimal hepatic metabolism and have no active metabolites covering the trough.
Only free, unbound drug acts, so protein binding does not supply activity during the trough.
Aminoglycosides are hydrophilic with a low volume of distribution, not lipophilic drugs that accumulate in tissue.
Aminoglycosides are cleared by glomerular filtration, which is why the nomogram adjusts for renal function.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man with methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia has had negative blood cultures after 3 days of oxacillin 2 g intravenously every 4 hours. The team proposes lengthening the interval to every 6 hours for convenience. The reference table lists the post-antibiotic effect of this drug class against Gram-positive organisms as roughly 2 hours.

Which action is most appropriate?
choices: Stop therapy now that blood cultures are negative
Lengthen the interval, since the effect lasts beyond 6 hours
Lengthen the interval to every 8 hours for the same reason
Keep the current interval, since the effect is short
Switch to a single large daily dose of the same drug

explain.html:
The post-antibiotic effect is the time bacteria take to recover and begin regrowing after drug exposure, and it decides how far concentrations can fall below the MIC between doses. It differs by class: prolonged for aminoglycosides against Gram-negatives, strong for fluoroquinolones, moderate for macrolides, and minimal (about 2 hours) for beta-lactams against Gram-positives. Beta-lactams are also time dependent, so their efficacy rests on keeping free drug above the MIC. The lecture's application is that a minimal PAE means frequent dosing is required.

Oxacillin is a beta-lactam treating MSSA, a Gram-positive, so its buffer after levels fall is only about 2 hours. Stretching the interval from every 4 to every 6 hours would leave hours below the MIC with regrowth, so the team should maintain the every 4 hour interval. Convenience does not outweigh time above the MIC in bacteremia.

The beta-lactam PAE is about 2 hours, far shorter than 6 hours.
An 8 hour interval would leave even longer below the MIC for a drug with a short PAE.
A single large daily dose suits concentration-dependent drugs with a long PAE, not a beta-lactam.
explain.takeaway: Beta-lactams have a minimal post-antibiotic effect (about 2 hours against Gram-positives), so their dosing interval must stay short.

questions.stem:
Two antibiotics have identical total serum concentrations in a patient and identical minimum inhibitory concentrations against the infecting organism. Drug 1 is bound to plasma proteins to a high degree, while drug 2 is bound only slightly. Both drugs reach the infected tissue in proportion to their unbound fraction.

Which statement best predicts their relative antibacterial activity?
choices: Drug 1 is more active, since binding prolongs its presence
Activity depends only on the route of elimination
Protein binding changes the organism's minimum inhibitory concentration
They are equally active, since total concentrations match
Drug 2 is more active, since only unbound drug acts

explain.html:
Protein binding is one of the pharmacokinetic factors that decides how much drug can act, because only free, unbound drug is capable of exerting an antimicrobial effect. Bound drug is held in plasma and cannot reach or act on the organism. That is why every pharmacodynamic index is written with free drug: fT>MIC, fCmax:MIC and fAUC:MIC. Total serum concentration can therefore overstate the active exposure of a highly bound drug.

Here the two drugs match on total concentration and on MIC, so the only difference is binding. Drug 2 is only slightly bound and has the larger unbound fraction reaching the tissue, so it is the more active. When comparing drugs or doses, the question to ask is how much free drug sits above the MIC.
why: Bound drug cannot act on the organism, so heavy binding lowers rather than raises activity.
The elimination route guides dosing in organ failure but does not decide the active fraction here.
The MIC is a property of the organism and the drug in vitro and is not changed by binding in the patient.
Equal total concentrations hide unequal free concentrations.
explain.takeaway: Only free, unbound drug has antimicrobial activity, so at equal total concentrations the less protein-bound drug is more active.

explain.objective: Apply pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) principles: Describe PK factors (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, tissue penetration).

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old man in the intensive care unit has Pseudomonas aeruginosa pneumonia. The isolate's ceftazidime MIC is 8 mg/L. The team models three ceftazidime regimens that each deliver 6 g per day and reports free (unbound) drug levels:

A pharmacist notes that regimen 1 exceeds a peak-to-MIC ratio of 10.

Regimen 1: 6 g once daily over 30 minutes; free peak 240 mg/L; free level above 8 mg/L for 7 of 24 hours.Regimen 2: 2 g every 8 hours over 30 minutes; free peak 80 mg/L; above 8 mg/L for 4 of each 8 hours.Regimen 3: 2 g every 8 hours infused over 4 hours; free peak 35 mg/L; above 8 mg/L for 7 of each 8 hours.

Which regimen is most likely to kill this organism best, and why?
choices: Regimen 1, since its free peak is 30 times the MIC
Any of them, since all three give the same total daily exposure
Regimen 3, since free drug stays above the MIC for longest
Regimen 1, since a long post-antibiotic effect covers the gap
Regimen 2, since its peak stays far above four times the MIC

explain.html:
Antibiotics fall into pharmacodynamic groups by what predicts their killing. For time-dependent drugs, the classic example being beta-lactams, the index is fT>MIC, the percent of the dosing interval that free drug stays above the MIC; increasing concentrations beyond about four times the MIC does not increase the rate of killing. The dosing goal is to keep free drug above the MIC for 40 to 70% of the interval depending on the class, about 60 to 70% for cephalosporins. Concentration-dependent drugs such as aminoglycosides instead target a peak:MIC of 8 to 10:1, and beta-lactams have only a minimal post-antibiotic effect, so they need frequent dosing or prolonged infusions.

Here all three regimens give 6 g per day, but only the 4-hour infusion keeps free ceftazidime above the MIC of 8 mg/L for most of each interval (about 88%). Regimen 1's impressive 30:1 peak is the red herring: that number matters for aminoglycosides, and the drug spends 17 hours below the MIC. This is why some beta-lactams, ceftazidime included, are given as continuous or prolonged infusions.
explain.table:
Regimen (6 g/day)Free peak : MICFree drug above MICMeets 60 to 70% goal?
1: 6 g once daily30 : 17 of 24 h (about 29%)No
2: 2 g every 8 h, 30-min infusion10 : 14 of 8 h (50%)No
3: 2 g every 8 h, 4-h infusionabout 4 : 17 of 8 h (about 88%)Yes
why: A large peak:MIC ratio is the goal for concentration-dependent drugs, while this beta-lactam is below the MIC 71% of the day.
Equal daily AUC does not equalize beta-lactam killing, which depends on time above the MIC.
Beta-lactams have a minimal post-antibiotic effect (about 2 hours), far short of the 17-hour gap.
Peaks beyond four times the MIC add little for a time-dependent drug, and regimen 2 is above the MIC only 50% of the time.
explain.takeaway: Beta-lactams are time-dependent: efficacy follows fT>MIC (about 60 to 70% for cephalosporins), so the same daily dose given as a prolonged infusion outperforms large infrequent doses.

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old man has osteomyelitis of the calcaneus 3 weeks after stepping on a nail through his sneaker. Bone biopsy grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa, susceptible to levofloxacin with an MIC of 2 mg/L, and he is started on levofloxacin. There is no abscess or retained foreign body. Peak serum levofloxacin is 8 mg/L, and the trough falls below 2 mg/L for part of each day. The reference bone-to-serum ratio for levofloxacin is 0.75. After 2 weeks he has improved only slightly. A resident proposes giving the same daily amount as smaller doses more often so the level never drops below the MIC.

Which adjustment is most likely to improve killing at the site of infection?
choices: Keep the regimen unchanged, since the isolate is susceptible
Give the same daily amount as smaller, more frequent doses
Switch to gentamicin, since hydrophilic drugs reach bone well
Raise the levofloxacin dose to increase exposure in bone
Switch to vancomycin, since it reaches bone better than this

explain.html:
The infection site decides whether a regimen reaches enough drug, and different tissues are penetrated to different degrees, so specific tissue penetration may require dose adjustment to reach the needed concentration there. Bone is a hard site: the bone-to-serum ratio is 0.75 for levofloxacin, about 0.2 for vancomycin, 0.1 to 0.3 for most beta-lactams, and predicted very low for aminoglycosides because they are highly hydrophilic. How to raise exposure depends on the drug's PD index. Beta-lactams are time-dependent (fT>MIC) and benefit from frequent dosing, but fluoroquinolones follow fAUC:MIC with concentration-dependent killing and a prolonged post-antibiotic effect, so their paradigm is flexible, high dose.

Here the bone level is about 8 x 0.75 = 6 mg/L, only 3 times the MIC of 2, which fits the slow response. The trough dipping below the MIC is the red herring, because time above MIC is not what drives fluoroquinolone killing and the post-antibiotic effect covers the low period. Raising the dose increases bone exposure relative to the MIC, which is the change most likely to help.
explain.table:
DrugBone:serum ratioWhy
Levofloxacin0.75Lipophilic, high volume of distribution
Vancomycinabout 0.20Higher doses needed in bone
Most beta-lactams0.1 to 0.3Hydrophilic, limited penetration
AminoglycosidesPredicted very lowHighly hydrophilic
why: Susceptible reflects standard serum exposure, and the bone level is only about 3 times the MIC.
Splitting the dose serves time above MIC, which is not the fluoroquinolone index, and it lowers the peaks without adding exposure.
Aminoglycosides are highly hydrophilic, with very low predicted bone penetration.
Vancomycin's bone ratio (about 0.2) is lower than levofloxacin's, and it does not treat Pseudomonas.
explain.takeaway: Fluoroquinolone efficacy follows fAUC:MIC, so when bone (or another poorly penetrated site) yields a low concentration relative to the MIC, increasing the dose, not the dosing frequency, raises site exposure.
